html:
Majapahit was a Hindu-Buddhist empire based in East Java, from 1293 to about 1527. At its peak in the 14th century it claimed overlordship over most of the islands of what are now Indonesia and Malaysia, though how far its real power reached is debated.

It was born out of the Mongol invasion of Java. In 1292 Kublai Khan sent a fleet to punish the king of Singhasari, who had insulted his envoys, but that king had already been killed by a rebel. His son-in-law Raden Wijaya allied with the Mongols to defeat the rebel, then turned on them and drove them out. In 1293 he founded Majapahit, named after a bitter fruit, near modern Mojokerto.

Its golden age came in the mid-14th century:

  • Under Queen Tribhuwana and her son Hayam Wuruk, king from 1350 to 1389, it fought campaigns across the archipelago.
  • The chief minister Gajah Mada is said to have sworn the Palapa oath, to give up spice until the islands were united.
  • The court poem Nagarakretagama of 1365 lists 98 tributaries from Sumatra to New Guinea.

It controlled much of the spice and rice trade. After Hayam Wuruk's death a civil war weakened it, and new Muslim port states on Java's north coast, led by the Demak Sultanate, grew richer as trade shifted to the Malacca Sultanate. Demak brought Majapahit down around 1527. Many of its nobles and priests are said to have fled to Bali, which kept its Hindu culture. Indonesian nationalists later held up Majapahit, with Srivijaya, as a model of a united archipelago.
